choices.english: the one group, as it were, out of error and false worship ...; the other, who were schooled under the Law
choices.why: οἱ μέν are the Greeks, out of idolatry; οἱ δέ the Jews, trained by the Law.

choices.why: ὀλίγα φροντίζω, to care little for; with Philippians 3:8.
μεστόω, to fill; ἀχλύς, mist, darkness.

pass_a_gloss: [opens inside the lemma begun in the previous section: 'Who shone in'] our hearts (καρδία) toward illumination (φωτισμός) of the knowledge (γνῶσις) of the glory of God in face (πρόσωπον) [stray numeral 9 omitted] of Jesus Christ.' That the faith (πίστις) [is] into God, even if it is practised (πράσσω, opt. pass.) in the face of Christ, the initiator (μυσταγωγός) will make clear (σαφηνίζω, fut.) through the phrase (λέξις) set before [us]; for both Jews and Greeks have been called (καλέω, pf. pass.) to full knowledge (ἐπίγνωσις) of Christ, the ones (οἱ μέν) as from error (πλάνη) and false worship (λατρεία) into the true knowledge of God (θεογνωσία), the others (οἱ δέ), being led by a tutor (παιδαγωγέω) in the law, into a more exact (ἀκριβής, comp.) knowing (εἴδησις) than that in the law. For this reason also the inspired (θεσπέσιος) Paul, 'on account of the surpassing (ὑπερέχω) of the knowledge' of Christ, is seen (ὁράω, pass.) as having cared (φροντίζω, pf.) little for the lessons (μάθημα) in the law. When therefore the initiators preach (κηρύσσω) Christ, and those believing into God believe into the one and true God truly, how is Christ not God, not bastard (νόθος), not falsely named (ψευδώνυμος), or of other nature (ἑτεροφυής) beside the Father, but rather true as from him by nature? For with an intelligible (νοητός) mist (ἀχλύς) and demonic (δαιμονιώδης) deceit (ἀπάτη) the mind of those wandering (πλανάω, pass.) has been filled (μεστόω, pf. pass.), but God promised (ἐπαγγέλλομαι, impf.) that from darkness (σκότος) the light would shine out (ἀναλάμπω, fut.) for us; for he said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah: 'The people (λαός) sitting in darkness, see [col. 343] a great light; those dwelling (κατοικέω) in land (χώρα) and shadow (σκιά) of death, light will shine (λάμπω, fut.) on you.' And the inspired David says, as from the person (πρόσωπον) of those in mist and darkness: 'For you will light (φωτίζω, fut.) my lamp (λύχνος), Lord; my God, you will light up my darkness.' And since the promise (ὑπόσχεσις) of the Father has now been fulfilled (πληρόω, pf. pass.) upon us, and the divine and intelligible light has shone through (διαυγάζω) for us, we have known (γινώσκω, pf.) his glory in face of Christ; then, if Christ is not God by nature and truly, have we beheld (θεάομαι, pf.) the glory of the Father in him? And yet I hear clearly the God and Father saying: 'My glory I will not give to another (ἕτερος)'; but see, he has given it to the Son; he is not, then, other beside him, except as far as in hypostasis (ὑπόστασις) and the existing individually (ἰδικῶς), so that the Father may not appear to have spoken falsely (ψευδοεπέω), having set forth (προτίθημι) his own glory in the face of the Son, and that he is God by nature, being known both in him and through him; for he is face and image (εἰκών) and radiance (ἀπαύγασμα) of his hypostasis; and the Son is revealed (ἀποκαλύπτω, pass.) by the Father, and he himself also reveals to us in himself the Father. Volume 3, Discourse 1. 'In earthen (ὀστράκινος) vessels (σκεῦος).' Earthen vessels he names the commonness (τὸ κοινόν) of the speech (λέξις); for not in pomp (κόμπος) of words [is] the handing down (παράδοσις) to us of the divine mysteries, but as in the speech accustomed (κατεθίζω, pf. pass.) to all, so that all may learn (μανθάνω) and understand (νοέω). What then, O Paul? For was it not attainable (ἐφικτός) for God, who makes all wise (σοφόω), to show the holy apostles very well-spoken (εὔστομος, superl.) easily, and much more fluent (κατευγλωττίζομαι, pf. pass.) than those, and knowing how to stun (καταπλήσσω) with din (κτύπος) of words those who meet (ἐντυγχάνω) [them]? Yes, he says, for he himself is the supplier (χορηγός) of the wisdom; but in earthen vessels, that is, in a small habit (ἕξις; probably read λέξει μικρᾷ, 'humble speech'), he shut up (κατακλείω) the divine treasure (θησαυρός) for us. On account of what cause? 'So that the excess (ὑπερβολή) of the power may be of God and not from us.' For thus they persuaded (πείθω) all to run to (προστρέχω) the faith. For if the word (λόγος) in them had been brilliant (λαμπρός), it would sometimes have seemed that the faith of those called had not been the achievement (κατόρθωσις) of his power. But since they persuaded through bare (ψιλός) words, no one doubts (ἐνδοιάζω) that the excess of the power in this has been God's. Earthen vessels we call the bodies (σῶμα) we wear around (περίκειμαι), being among the things of sense (αἰσθητός), with this meaning (διάνοια): since, still wearing the flesh that hinders (ἐμποδίζω) the contemplation (θεωρία) of the truth, we have the knowledge about the Trinity (Τριάς), the excess of the greatness (μέγεθος) of the knowledge is made known (γνωρίζω, pass.) to us as being not from us, but from power of God. [col. 345] 'In every [way] being afflicted (θλίβω, pass.), but not being crushed (στενοχωρέω, pass.), etc.' [stray numeral 10 omitted] For they are seen to have endured (ἀνατλάω) even death itself on behalf of the piety (εὐσέβεια) toward him; yet even if it befell (συμβαίνω) them to suffer this, still they live, being about to live to God; and, as the word (λόγος) of the wisdom says: 'They seemed (δοκέω) in [the] eyes of men' [cut off; the quotation continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: …our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

By this phrase our guide into the mysteries makes clear that faith is directed to God, even when it is exercised in the face of Christ. For both Jews and Greeks have been called to the knowledge of Christ: the one group, as it were, out of error and false worship into the true knowledge of God; the other, who were schooled under the Law, into a knowledge more exact than that of the Law. That is why the inspired Paul too is seen to have cared little for the lessons of the Law, “because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge” of Christ (Philippians 3:8).

Since, then, the guides into the mysteries preach Christ, and those who believe in God believe in the one God, and believe truly, how is Christ not God? He is not spurious, not falsely so called, not of another nature than the Father; rather, He is true God, as being from Him by nature.

The mind of those who go astray is filled with a darkness of the mind and with demonic deceit, but God promised that light would shine out of darkness for us (2 Corinthians 4:6). For He said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, “The people that sits in darkness, see a great light; you who dwell in the land and shadow of death, a light will shine on you” (Isaiah 9:2). And the inspired David says, as if speaking for those in gloom and darkness, “For You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, You will light up my darkness” (Psalm 18:28). Since the Father’s promise has now been fulfilled in us, and the divine light, seen by the mind, has dawned on us, we have come to know His glory in the face of Christ.

And then, if Christ is not God by nature and in truth, how have we beheld the Father’s glory in Him? Yet I plainly hear God the Father say, “My glory I will not give to another” (Isaiah 42:8); and see, He has given it to the Son. The Son, then, is not other than He, except in His own hypostasis and in His distinct existence; otherwise the Father would seem to have spoken falsely when He set His own glory in the face of the Son. It shows, too, that He who is God by nature is known both in Him and through Him. For the Son is the face and image and radiance of His hypostasis (Hebrews 1:3). The Son is revealed by the Father, and He in turn reveals the Father to us in Himself (Matthew 11:27).

“In earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). He calls the plainness of his speech “earthen vessels.” For the divine mysteries were not handed down to us in pompous words, but in the language that everyone is used to, so that all might learn and understand.

What then, Paul? Was it not within the power of God, who makes all wise, to make the holy apostles exceedingly eloquent with ease, far more polished in speech than those others, and skilled at stunning their hearers with the din of words? “Yes,” he says, “for He Himself is the giver of wisdom.” But He has shut up the divine treasure for us in earthen vessels, that is, in a lowly form. For what reason? “So that the surpassing greatness of the power may be of God and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

For in this way the apostles persuaded all to run to the faith. If their speech had been brilliant, it might at times have seemed that the faith of those who were called was not the work of His power. But since they persuaded with plain words, no one doubts that the surpassing power at work in this came from God.

By “earthen vessels” we mean the bodies we wear while we live among the things of sense, and we mean it in this way: since, while still clothed in flesh, which hinders the contemplation of the truth, we have the knowledge of the Trinity, the surpassing greatness of this knowledge is made known to us as coming not from ourselves but from the power of God.
“We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed,” and so on (2 Corinthians 4:8).

For they are seen to have endured even death itself for the sake of their devotion to Him. Yet even if this befell them, still they live, since they are to live to God. And, as the book of Wisdom says, “In the eyes of men they seemed…” (Wisdom of Solomon 3:2).
